The browser can cache the file indefinitely, and when the content changes, the hash changes, producing a new URL that forces a fresh download. Public-folder files keep their exact names, so they cannot benefit from this automatic cache invalidation.

followUps.question: Where would you put a robots.txt or sitemap?
followUps.answer: Traditionally in the public folder so they are served at the fixed URLs /robots.txt and /sitemap.xml. The App Router also supports generating them in code via special files like robots.ts and sitemap.ts, which produce the same routes dynamically. Either way, the goal is a predictable, root-level URL that crawlers expect.

question: How do you read URL parameters and query strings in the App Router?
directAnswer: Page components receive a params prop for dynamic route segments and a searchParams prop for the query string. In current Next.js both are promises you await. In Client Components you use the useParams and useSearchParams hooks from next/navigation instead.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: params holds the values of dynamic route segments, like the slug in /blog/[slug]. searchParams holds the query string values, like ?page=2. These give your page access to the variable parts of the URL so it can render the right content.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Pages need to know which record to show and what filters or pagination to apply, all of which come from the URL. Providing them as props (server) or hooks (client) gives a consistent way to read them depending on where the code runs.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A Server Component page receives params and searchParams as props; in current versions these are promises, so you await them, for example const { slug } = await params. Reading searchParams makes the route dynamic since it depends on the request. In Client Components you cannot receive these as props directly for the query string, so you use useSearchParams and useParams from next/navigation, which read them reactively in the browser.

whyImportant: Reading params and query strings is needed for almost any data-driven page, and the server-versus-client difference is a common source of confusion. Interviewers check that you know both paths and that searchParams affects rendering mode.
realWorldExample: A search results page at /search reads searchParams.q for the query and searchParams.page for pagination, fetches matching results on the server, and renders them. A client-side filter sidebar uses useSearchParams to read and update the query as the user changes filters.

nestedTopics.title: params for dynamic segments
nestedTopics.explanation: params contains the values of bracketed route segments, keyed by the segment name. For /products/[id], params.id is the product id. In the App Router page components await params since it is a promise.

nestedTopics.title: searchParams for query strings
nestedTopics.explanation: searchParams contains the parsed query string. Reading it in a page makes that route dynamic because the output depends on the request URL, so the page is rendered per request rather than statically.

nestedTopics.title: Client hooks
nestedTopics.explanation: In Client Components you use useSearchParams and useParams from next/navigation to read the URL reactively, since client components cannot receive the server-provided params and searchParams props for this purpose.

followUps.question: Why does reading searchParams make a route dynamic?
followUps.answer: Because the query string is part of the incoming request and can differ per visit, so Next.js cannot pre-render a single static version that is correct for all queries. Once a page depends on searchParams, it must render per request to reflect the actual query, which makes it dynamic rather than statically generated.

followUps.question: How do you read the query string in a Client Component?
followUps.answer: You use the useSearchParams hook from next/navigation, which returns a read-only URLSearchParams-like object you can call get on. Client components do not receive the searchParams prop, so this hook is the way. For dynamic route segments in a client component, you use the useParams hook similarly.

followUps.question: Why are params and searchParams promises now?
followUps.answer: Recent Next.js versions made them asynchronous to support streaming and to defer resolving request data until it is actually needed, which improves performance and enables more dynamic behavior. As a result, page components await them, and code written for older versions that read them synchronously must be updated to await the values.
